clue.text: Distracted if recent changes are implemented

indicators.note: the letters of the words if recent undergo changes, which tells us to rearrange them

explanation.surface: Someone is driven to distraction when the latest reforms are put into effect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes are implemented' signals that the letters of IF RECENT are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Frantic, wildly agitated behaviour is that of someone distracted, in the old sense of driven out of their wits.

clue.text: Payment to Russians to get leader out of problems

indicators.note: the leading letter of the synonym for problems is to be taken out

parts.note: problems are troubles

explanation.surface: Russia is paid off so that its head of state escapes from difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get leader out of' removes the first letter, T, from TROUBLES. 'Leader' sounds political in the surface but just means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Russian currency is counted in these units, so they are what you pay Russians in.

clue.text: Odd thing, to collapse at the end of the day

indicators.note: odd suggests the letters of thing are made strange, i.e. rearranged

parts.note: to collapse is to fall

explanation.surface: Something strange keels over once the day is done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' rearranges THING to NIGHT; FALL (collapse) is placed at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Dusk, when darkness comes on, marks the close of daylight hours.

clue.text: Passionate Dickensian character changed ends

indicators.note: the first and last letters of the character's name swap places

parts.note: William Dorrit, father of Little Dorrit in the Dickens novel

explanation.surface: A fervent figure from Dickens had a change of heart at both ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed ends' swaps the D and T at the ends of DORRIT. Little Dorrit is a Charles Dickens novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Torrid love affairs are hot and intense, full of passion.

clue.text: Jumblies unlikely to be thus surprised?

definitions.text: Jumblies unlikely to be thus surprised?

parts.words: Jumblies unlikely to be thus surprised?
parts.note: Edward Lear's Jumblies have blue hands, so if caught in the act their hands would be blue, not the usual colour of guilt

explanation.surface: Lear's nonsense creatures would hardly be caught out in this particular way.
explanation.walkthrough: In Edward Lear's poem The Jumblies, 'their heads are green, and their hands are blue', so they could only be caught blue-handed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being discovered in the very act of wrongdoing is the idiom's meaning, with the hands imagined stained with blood.

clue.text: Sign language intelligible to book people

definitions.text: Sign language intelligible to book people

parts.words: Sign language intelligible to book people
parts.note: book people are bookmakers at the racecourse, who signal odds to one another with arm and hand gestures

explanation.surface: A form of signing that only bookish types can follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'book people' suggests readers or librarians, but here it means bookies, who take bets; their semaphore of arm signals at British racecourses has this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Racecourse bookmakers use a code of hand signals to pass on betting odds across the ring.

clue.text: Tree taking the, lead in drama, perhaps

indicators.note: the lead of the word the is its first letter
perhaps indicates the letters could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A tree is cast as the leading player in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead' takes T from 'the'; 'perhaps' rearranges IN + DRAMA to AMARIND. 'taking' just joins, and 'lead in drama' misleads as a starring role.
explanation.definitionFit: This tropical tree bears pods whose sour pulp is used in cooking.

clue.text: Becomes fond of fleas, to judge by the sound

definitions.text: fleas, to judge by the sound

explanation.surface: A person warms to parasites, judging by how they sound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fleas' sounds like 'flees', and someone who flees takes to their heels (or takes to flight), so the second reading is a playful sound-alike definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To warm to someone or start liking something; and one who runs off may be said to head for the hills in this phrase.

clue.text: Craft in a river can put about

indicators.note: the word can is put around the other pieces, enclosing them

parts.note: the Tamar is the river dividing Devon and Cornwall

explanation.surface: A boat on a river changes course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put about' sounds nautical, turning a boat, but signals enclosing. The River Tamar runs between Devon and Cornwall in England.
explanation.definitionFit: A twin-hulled boat is a type of vessel, and craft means a vessel.

clue.text: Thief whose tears are insincere?

explanation.surface: A robber who weeps only for show.
explanation.walkthrough: A mugger is also an Indian crocodile, and crocodile tears are famously false.
explanation.definitionFit: A street robber who attacks people; and a broad-snouted Indian crocodile, the animal behind the idiom of fake weeping.

clue.text: More expensive as result of increase EEC added

parts.note: an increase is a rise, as in a pay up
the European Economic Community was known as the Common Market

explanation.surface: Prices rise as a result of a rise when Britain joined Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: The EEC, forerunner of the EU, was popularly called the Common Market in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Upmarket goods aim at wealthier buyers and so carry higher prices.

clue.text: Their views, in the main, are one-sided

definitions.text: Their views, in the main, are one-sided

parts.words: Their views, in the main, are one-sided
parts.note: the main is the sea; these sea creatures have both eyes on one side of the head

explanation.surface: Their opinions are mostly biased.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the main' looks like 'mostly' but means 'in the sea'; plaice and sole see from one side only.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaice, sole and flounder are bottom-dwelling fish with both eyes on one side of a flattened body.

clue.text: Rescue children's author, say

indicators.note: say indicates the word sounds like the author's name spoken

parts.note: Arthur Ransome wrote Swallows and Amazons

explanation.surface: An instruction to save a writer of books for young readers.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ransome wrote the Swallows and Amazons books; his surname sounds identical to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay to free a captive is to redeem or rescue them.

clue.text: It can provide actors with no end of excitement

definitions.text: It can provide actors with no end of excitement

parts.words: It can provide actors with no end of excitement
parts.note: the reading is of a Hollywood statuette that thrills any performer who wins one

explanation.surface: Something that thrills performers endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Academy Award statuette is a film actor's highest prize.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Award statuette brings an actor enormous delight on winning.

clue.text: How unfittingly one suits oneself!

parts.note: suits oneself means buys a suit, and unfittingly means without a tailor's fitting: ready-made clothing

explanation.surface: An exclamation at how selfishly someone pleases themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suits oneself' looks like 'does as one likes', but means kitting oneself out in a suit bought ready-made, with no fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready-made clothes are bought from the rail rather than tailored to measure.

clue.text: Knave, perhaps? Certainly not King or Queen

definitions.text: Knave, perhaps? Certainly not King or Queen

parts.words: Knave, perhaps? Certainly not King or Queen
parts.note: a knave is a rogue, while the monarch can do no wrong by constitutional maxim

explanation.surface: A jack in a card pack, as opposed to the higher court cards.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests playing cards; in fact a knave is a rogue, and the British maxim says 'the King can do no wrong'.
explanation.definitionFit: A knave is an old word for a dishonest rascal, one who commits offences.

clue.text: Twenty years after brought him to book again

definitions.text: Twenty years after brought him to book again

parts.words: Twenty years after brought him to book again
parts.note: Twenty Years After is Dumas's sequel to The Three Musketeers, which returned its Gascon hero to print

explanation.surface: Two decades on, a person is finally held to account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought him to book' looks like 'punished him', but Twenty Years After is the Dumas sequel that put the musketeer back in a book.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero of Dumas's musketeer novels reappears in their sequel set two decades later.

clue.text: Fellow challengin' bureaucrat

parts.note: a fellow is a man
challenging is daring, so with the final g dropped it is darin'

explanation.surface: A man defying an official.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped g of 'challengin'' tells you to drop the g of 'daring' too.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior civil servant is called this, after the officials of imperial China.

clue.text: To play trick on tough could be rash

parts.note: to play a trick on someone is to fool them
tough means hardy

explanation.surface: Playing pranks on a hard man might be reckless.
explanation.definitionFit: Recklessly bold behaviour is rash, taking needless risks.

clue.text: Seafood a tearful diner ate with chips

definitions.text: Seafood a tearful diner ate with chips

parts.words: Seafood a tearful diner ate with chips
parts.note: in Lewis Carroll's poem the Walrus weeps as he eats the shellfish he has lured along the beach

explanation.surface: A sad customer had fish and chips.
explanation.walkthrough: The tearful diner is the Walrus in Carroll's The Walrus and the Carpenter, who weeps while eating; 'chips' recalls British fish and chips, and the Walrus talks of 'cabbages and kings' with the shellfish.
explanation.definitionFit: These bivalve molluscs are seafood, and the Walrus ate them all.

clue.text: Naive about inside information

indicators.note: inside indicates one piece is put within the word for information

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Being innocent about inside knowledge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside information' looks like a single phrase, but 'inside' is the container signal; GEN is British slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone inexperienced and gullible is called this, like unripe fruit.

clue.text: Most favourable environment for a sub-group

explanation.surface: The best habitat for a small subset.
explanation.walkthrough: One is 'in one's element' when in favourable surroundings; and a member or part of a larger set is also this.
explanation.definitionFit: A natural habitat where one thrives; and a component part of a larger whole.

clue.text: Will drink in the shade

explanation.surface: A bequest of something to drink in the shadow.
explanation.walkthrough: A triple definition: resolve, a strong alcoholic drink, and a ghost (a 'shade' in poetic usage). 'in the' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Will means determination or resolve; drink here is hard liquor; a shade is a ghost.

clue.text: Poet hides letters about love

indicators.note: about indicates the rearranged letters go around the other piece
the letters of hides are to be rearranged

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A writer conceals love letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letters' rearranges HIDES to HESID, which goes 'about' O (love, nil in tennis).
explanation.definitionFit: This early Greek wrote Works and Days and the Theogony in verse.

clue.text: Split atom to get half of it

definitions.text: Split atom to get half of it

parts.words: Split atom to get half of it
parts.note: split the word atom into A TO M, which is half of the set of letters from A to Z

explanation.surface: Splitting the atom yields only half of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split atom' suggests physics; splitting the word gives A TO M, the first half of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The set of letters from A to Z is the writing system's sequence of characters.

clue.text: Boy who reconnoitres should be so willing

definitions.text: Boy who reconnoitres should be so

explanation.surface: A lad on reconnaissance ought to be ready and eager.
explanation.walkthrough: The Boy Scout motto is 'Be prepared'; the scout is the boy who reconnoitres.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scouts' motto tells members to be ready; and being ready to do something means being willing.

clue.text: Soldier who gives order?

explanation.surface: A military man who issues commands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives order' sounds like commanding, but means putting things in order, ranking them.
explanation.definitionFit: A private, or an officer promoted from the ranks; and one who ranks, arranging things in sequence.

clue.text: Braggart such as 15

explanation.surface: A show-off like the musketeer of the other clue.
explanation.walkthrough: People from Gascony in south-west France were proverbially boastful, and D'Artagnan came from there.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of Gascony were reputed boasters, hence the word for a braggart; and D'Artagnan was one by birth.

clue.text: Set off for school in time

indicators.note: in tells us the school's name goes inside the word for time

parts.note: a date is a point in time
Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: Leaving for school on time.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton College is the elite English boarding school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: To explode a bomb is to set it off.
